title: "The Triangle of Everything"
engine: markdown
pyodide:
  packages:
    - numpy
    - pandas
    - altair
---

In 2023, two astrophysicists published a chart that placed **every
object in the Universe on one pair of axes**: quarks, viruses, fleas,
whales, planets, stars, black holes, galaxies, and the observable Universe
itself (Lineweaver & Patel, *All objects and some questions*, American
Journal of Physics 91:819). In this part you will rebuild that chart, step by step.



```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
import js
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import altair as alt
from pyodide.http import open_url

# Data files live beside this page; the Python worker runs from site_libs/.
DATA_URL = js.location.href.split("site_libs/")[0] + "data/"

alt.data_transformers.enable("default", max_rows=12_000)

# Physical constants, cgs units (grams, centimetres, seconds)
G    = 6.674e-8       # gravitational constant [cm^3 g^-1 s^-2]
c    = 2.998e10       # speed of light [cm/s]
hbar = 1.055e-27      # reduced Planck constant [erg s]
H0   = 70 / 3.086e19  # Hubble constant: 70 km/s/Mpc, converted to [1/s]

print("Environment ready.")
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| include: false
# Pre-build every name the page uses, so each cell works no matter which
# cells were run before it. The visible cells re-derive all of this.
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv").read()
objects = pd.read_csv(open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv"))
rows = objects.astype(str).values.tolist()
names  = objects["name"].tolist()
groups = objects["group"].tolist()
mass   = objects["mass_g"].to_numpy()
radius = objects["radius_cm"].to_numpy()

group_colours = {
    "particles":         "#767676",
    "life":              "#00A676",
    "worlds":            "#1D5FD1",
    "stars":             "#E49B0F",
    "black holes":       "#111111",
    "cosmic structures": "#C0448F",
}

# Reserved for reference lines: neither colour appears in the object palette.
DENSITY_COLOURS = {
    "atomic density":  "#6F2DA8",
    "nuclear density": "#B2182B",
}

LABEL_PLACEMENTS = {
    "top quark":           ("right", -8, -11),
    "Higgs boson":         ("right", -8,  11),
    "stellar black hole":  ("right", -8, -22),
    "neutron star":        ("right", -8, -13),
    "white dwarf":         ("right", -8,   1),
    "brown dwarf":         ("right", -8,   5),
    "Jupiter":             ("right", -8,  12),
    "red giant":           ("left",   8,  -4),
    "Sun":                 ("left",   8,  11),
    "Earth":               ("left",   8,   6),
    "Moon":                ("left",   8,   8),
    "Ceres":               ("left",   8,  11),
    "globular cluster":    ("right", -8,  15),
    "galaxy cluster":      ("right", -8, -12),
    "supercluster":        ("right", -8,  12),
    "observable Universe": ("right", -8,   0),
}

GROUP_DOMAIN = list(group_colours)
GROUP_RANGE = [group_colours[group] for group in GROUP_DOMAIN]

def cosmos_x(field="radius_cm"):
    return alt.X(
        f"{field}:Q",
        title="radius (cm)",
        scale=alt.Scale(type="log", domain=[1e-35, 1e30], nice=False),
        axis=alt.Axis(grid=True, tickCount=14, format=".0e"),
    )

def cosmos_y(field="mass_g"):
    return alt.Y(
        f"{field}:Q",
        title="mass (g)",
        scale=alt.Scale(type="log", domain=[1e-40, 1e60], nice=False),
        axis=alt.Axis(grid=True, tickCount=11, format=".0e"),
    )

def group_colour(show_legend=True):
    legend = alt.Legend(
        title="Object group", orient="bottom",
        direction="horizontal", columns=3,
    ) if show_legend else None
    return alt.Color(
        "group:N",
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=GROUP_DOMAIN, range=GROUP_RANGE),
        legend=legend,
    )

def object_layers(table=objects, show_legend=True, point_size=55):
    points = alt.Chart(table).mark_circle(size=point_size).encode(
        x=cosmos_x(),
        y=cosmos_y(),
        color=group_colour(show_legend),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("name:N", title="Object"),
            alt.Tooltip("group:N", title="Group"),
            alt.Tooltip("mass_g:Q", title="Mass (g)", format=".2e"),
            alt.Tooltip("radius_cm:Q", title="Radius (cm)", format=".2e"),
        ],
    )

    label_table = table.copy()
    label_table["label_align"] = "left"
    label_table["label_dx"] = 8
    label_table["label_dy"] = 0

    for name, (align, dx, dy) in LABEL_PLACEMENTS.items():
        row = label_table["name"].eq(name)
        label_table.loc[row, ["label_align", "label_dx", "label_dy"]] = [
            align, dx, dy
        ]

    label_layers = []
    for (align, dx, dy), label_group in label_table.groupby(
        ["label_align", "label_dx", "label_dy"], sort=False
    ):
        label_base = alt.Chart(label_group).encode(
            x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="name:N"
        )
        label_layers.extend([
            label_base.mark_text(
                align=align, dx=dx, dy=dy, fontSize=11,
                color="white", stroke="white", strokeWidth=3,
            ),
            label_base.mark_text(
                align=align, dx=dx, dy=dy, fontSize=11,
            ).encode(color=group_colour(False)),
        ])

    return alt.layer(points, *label_layers)

r_line = np.logspace(-35, 30, 200)

def mass_at_density(rho, r):
    return 4/3 * np.pi * rho * r**3

def schwarzschild_mass(r):
    return r * c**2 / (2 * G)

def compton_mass(r):
    return hbar / (r * c)

rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)
l_p = np.sqrt(hbar * G / c**3)
m_p = np.sqrt(hbar * c / G)
r_x = np.sqrt(2 * G * hbar / c**3)
m_x = np.sqrt(hbar * c / (2 * G))
rho_human = rho_all[names.index("human")]
iU = names.index("observable Universe")
ratio = 2 * G * mass[iU] / c**2 / radius[iU]

density_lines = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({
        "radius_cm": r_line,
        "mass_g": mass_at_density(rho, r_line),
        "density": label,
    })
    for rho, label in [(1.0, "atomic density"),
                       (2.3e14, "nuclear density")]
], ignore_index=True)
density_line_base = alt.Chart(density_lines).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(),
    y=cosmos_y(),
)

atomic_density_line = density_line_base.transform_filter(
    alt.datum.density == "atomic density"
).mark_line(
    color=DENSITY_COLOURS["atomic density"],
    strokeDash=[8, 5], strokeWidth=2, clip=True,
)

nuclear_density_line = density_line_base.transform_filter(
    alt.datum.density == "nuclear density"
).mark_line(
    color=DENSITY_COLOURS["nuclear density"],
    strokeDash=[3, 3], strokeWidth=2, clip=True,
)

density_line_chart = atomic_density_line + nuclear_density_line

density_label_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": [3e18, 1e11],
    "mass_g": [mass_at_density(1, 3e18),
               mass_at_density(2.3e14, 1e11)],
    "label": ["atomic density", "nuclear density"],
})
atomic_density_label = alt.Chart(
    density_label_data.query("label == 'atomic density'")
).mark_text(
    align="left", dx=8, dy=15,
    color=DENSITY_COLOURS["atomic density"], fontSize=13,
    fontWeight="bold",
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

nuclear_density_label = alt.Chart(
    density_label_data.query("label == 'nuclear density'")
).mark_text(
    align="right", dx=-8, dy=14,
    color=DENSITY_COLOURS["nuclear density"], fontSize=13,
    fontWeight="bold",
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

density_labels = atomic_density_label + nuclear_density_label

wall_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": r_line,
    "gravity_mass_g": schwarzschild_mass(r_line),
    "compton_mass_g": compton_mass(r_line),
    "upper_mass_g": 1e60,
    "lower_mass_g": 1e-40,
})
gravity_region = alt.Chart(wall_data).mark_area(
    color="#e66852", opacity=0.15, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y("gravity_mass_g"),
    y2=alt.Y2("upper_mass_g:Q"),
)
quantum_region = alt.Chart(wall_data).mark_area(
    color="#4269d0", opacity=0.15, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y("lower_mass_g"),
    y2=alt.Y2("compton_mass_g:Q"),
)
wall_lines = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({"radius_cm": r_line,
                  "mass_g": schwarzschild_mass(r_line),
                  "wall": "black-hole limit"}),
    pd.DataFrame({"radius_cm": r_line,
                  "mass_g": compton_mass(r_line),
                  "wall": "Compton limit"}),
], ignore_index=True)
wall_line_chart = alt.Chart(wall_lines).mark_line(
    color="#171717", strokeWidth=1.5, clip=True
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), detail="wall:N")
```

## 1 · Everything in the Universe

What would a graph of everything compare?
Mass and radius are the two properties **every physical
object has**. But from a neutrino to the observable Universe, mass spans
about **90 orders of magnitude** and radius about **44**. This means both axes must be
logarithmic.

::: {.callout-tip title="Powers of Ten"}
Watch the nine-minute 1977 short film [*Powers of Ten*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0fKBhvDjuy0) before
continuing. Notice how changing scale changes which objects and relationships
can be seen.
:::

The chart's raw material is a curated table with one row per object; name,
group, mass and radius:

```{pyodide}
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv").read()
objects = pd.read_csv(open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv"))
rows = objects.astype(str).values.tolist()
names  = objects["name"].tolist()
groups = objects["group"].tolist()
mass   = objects["mass_g"].to_numpy()
radius = objects["radius_cm"].to_numpy()

print(f"{'name':<22} {'group':<18} {'mass':>13} {'radius':>14}")
print("-" * 70)
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r[0]:<22} {r[1]:<18} {float(r[2]):>10.2e} g {float(r[3]):>10.2e} cm")
print(f"\n{len(names)} objects in total")
```

```{pyodide}
assert len(names) == 29
assert mass.max() / mass.min() > 1e89
assert radius.max() / radius.min() > 1e43
print("✓ 29 objects; mass spans 90 orders of magnitude, radius spans 44")
```

Start with five more familiar objects:

```{pyodide}
FAMILIAR = ["flea", "human", "blue whale", "Earth", "Sun"]

familiar = objects[objects["name"].isin(FAMILIAR)]

familiar_base = alt.Chart(familiar).encode(
    x=alt.X("radius_cm:Q", title="radius (cm)",
            scale=alt.Scale(type="log", nice=False)),
    y=alt.Y("mass_g:Q", title="mass (g)",
            scale=alt.Scale(type="log", nice=False)),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("name:N", title="Object"),
        alt.Tooltip("mass_g:Q", title="Mass (g)", format=".2e"),
        alt.Tooltip("radius_cm:Q", title="Radius (cm)", format=".2e"),
    ],
)

familiar_points = familiar_base.mark_circle(size=80, color="#4269d0")
familiar_labels = familiar_base.mark_text(
    align="left", dx=7, fontSize=12, color="#4269d0"
).encode(text="name:N")

(familiar_points + familiar_labels).properties(
    width="container",
    height=420,
    title="Five familiar objects: 37 orders of magnitude in mass",
).configure_axis(
    gridColor="#dddddd", gridOpacity=0.7
).configure_title(
    fontSize=20,
    anchor="middle",
    offset=16,
)
```

Notice that they fall roughly on a straight line.

Before interpreting that line, ask what **radius** means for a human. A human
is not a sphere. The table assigns the human a mass of 70 kg and a radius of
50 cm, where 50 cm is a convenient measure of characteristic size. What would
happen if we mistakenly treated it as a literal spherical radius?

```{pyodide}
i = names.index("human")
sphere_volume_cm3 = 4/3 * np.pi * radius[i]**3
sphere_volume_litres = sphere_volume_cm3 / 1000
rho_human = mass[i] / sphere_volume_cm3

print(f"volume of a sphere with radius 50 cm: {sphere_volume_litres:.0f} litres")
print(f"70 kg divided by that volume: {rho_human:.2f} g/cm³")
```

::: {.callout-important title="Approximate Magnitude"}
A 70 kg human has a volume of roughly 70 litres because the human body is
close to the density of water. The calculation gives 524 litres only because
we forced the 50 cm characteristic size into a formula for a sphere. The
result does **not** show that humans have a density of 0.13 g/cm³.
Radius is a geometric measurement for a
planet or star, but an approximate characteristic size for an irregular object
such as a flea, human or whale. The chart is designed for comparisons across
many orders of magnitude, not precise estimates of each object's density.
:::

Why are these corners empty?

## 3 · Lines of constant density

Density is mass divided by volume:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}.$$

Here $\rho$ (the Greek letter *rho*) is density in grams per cubic centimetre,
$m$ is mass in grams, and $V$ is volume in cubic centimetres. Rearranging the
definition gives $m = \rho V$ (an object's mass is its density multiplied by
the space it occupies).

For a sphere of radius $r$, the volume is

$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3,$$

where $r$ is the radius in centimetres and $\pi$ is the geometric constant pi.
Substituting the sphere's volume into $m = \rho V$ gives

$$m = \frac{4}{3}\pi \rho r^3.$$

This is exact for a uniform sphere and an approximation when an irregular
object is represented by a characteristic radius and an average density.





At a
fixed density, doubling the radius multiplies the volume—and therefore the
mass—by $2^3 = 8$.

Taking logs gives $\log m = 3\log r + \text{constant}$. A constant-density
relationship therefore appears as a straight line with **slope 3 on the log–log chart**.

Different densities have the same slope but different vertical
positions.

**Atomic density** describes typical condensed atomic matter:
water, flesh, rock and many solids and liquids often
has an average density near $\rho \approx 1\ \text{g/cm}^3$. Its mass is spread
over the full volume occupied by atoms, including the space between
nucleus and electrons. Several familiar
condensed objects —-- viruses, animals, asteroids, planets and the Sun —-- fall near
the atomic-density line.

**Nuclear density** is about $2.3 \times 10^{14}\ \text{g/cm}^3$: fourteen
orders of magnitude greater. At this density protons and neutrons are packed together as they are
inside an atomic nucleus, so atoms no longer exist as
separate structures. One cubic centimetre would contain roughly 230
billion kilograms of matter. Atomic nuclei and neutron stars lie near this
density.

Most objects lie between the two lines. However, red giants, galaxy clusters and the
Universe have average densities far below the atomic line.


The proton and the neutron star both sit near
the nuclear-density line. A neutron star is matter at approximately the
density of an atomic nucleus, compressed into an object the size of a city.

```{pyodide}
rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)

i_ns, i_p = names.index("neutron star"), names.index("proton")
assert 1e14 < rho_all[i_ns] < 1e15 and 1e14 < rho_all[i_p] < 1e15
assert rho_all[names.index("red giant")] < 1e-5
print("✓ proton and neutron star both sit at nuclear density, ~10¹⁴ g/cm³")
print(f"densest object:  {names[int(np.argmax(rho_all))]}")
print(f"fluffiest object: {names[int(np.argmin(rho_all))]}")
```

The least dense thing in the Universe is (obviously?) **the
Universe itself**, about $10^{-29}\ \text{g/cm}^3$, six protons per cubic metre.

#### Densities {#sec-ex-density}

You have `rho_all` for all 29 objects. Rank everything by density and
print a table from densest to least dense, with the group and the density of
each object.

Which **group** is at the top of
the table?

A red giant has nearly te same *mass* as a white dwarf; what is the difference in density?

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_density
import js
import numpy as np
from pyodide.http import open_url
DATA_URL = js.location.href.split("site_libs/")[0] + "data/"
text = open_url(DATA_URL + "objects_universe.csv").read()
rows = [line.split(",") for line in text.strip().split("\n")[1:]]
names  = [r[0] for r in rows]
groups = [r[1] for r in rows]
mass   = np.array([float(r[2]) for r in rows])
radius = np.array([float(r[3]) for r in rows])
rho_all = mass / (4/3 * np.pi * radius**3)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_density
# `names`, `groups`, `mass`, `radius` and `rho_all` are all loaded.
# 1. Get the object order sorted by density, densest first.
# 2. Print rank, name, group, density for every object.
# 3. Compute the red giant / white dwarf density gap in decades.

order = ______

for rank, i in enumerate(order, 1):
    print(f"{rank:>2}. {names[i]:<20} {groups[i]:<18} {rho_all[i]:>9.1e} g/cm³")

gap = ______
print(f"\nred giant vs white dwarf: {gap:.0f} decades of density")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_density"}
**Hint 1**: `np.argsort(rho_all)` gives indices from *smallest* to
largest; reverse it with `[::-1]` to get densest first.
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_density"}
**Hint 2**: A "decade" is a factor of ten, so the gap in decades is
`np.log10(rho_wd / rho_rg)`. Get each with
`rho_all[names.index("white dwarf")]`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_density"}
**Fully worked solution:**

```python
order = np.argsort(rho_all)[::-1]

for rank, i in enumerate(order, 1):
    print(f"{rank:>2}. {names[i]:<20} {groups[i]:<18} {rho_all[i]:>9.1e} g/cm³")

gap = np.log10(rho_all[names.index("white dwarf")]
               / rho_all[names.index("red giant")])
print(f"\nred giant vs white dwarf: {gap:.0f} decades of density")
```

The top of the table belongs entirely to **particles**. The top quark
and Higgs boson are the densest "objects" plotted. The red giant and white dwarf differ by roughly **12 decades**
of density.
:::

## 4 · Two walls



There are no objects in the top-left (small but extremely heavy), or
in the bottom-right (huge but almost massless).

This is because physics bounds the set of feasible mass-radius pairings.

The bounds form two "walls":

**The gravity wall.** A mass $m$ becomes a black hole if compressed into a small enough radius; the Schwarzschild radius
$r_s = 2Gm/c^2$. For a given radius, the heaviest possible object is
$m = rc^2/2G$: **slope +1** on our axes. Black holes sit
exactly *on* this line, and nothing can go above it.

**The quantum wall.** According to quantum mechanics,  a particle of mass $m$ cannot be localised
below its Compton wavelength $\lambda_c = \hbar / mc$, so the lightest possible object of
radius $r$ is $m = \hbar/rc$: **slope −1**. Below this line, "object"
stops meaning anything. Fundamental particles (top quark, Higgs, electron,
neutrino) are plotted *on* their Compton wavelengths.

::: {.callout-note title="Why are the slopes +1 and −1?"}
On a log–log chart, define

$$x = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{r}{1\ \mathrm{cm}}\right), \qquad
y = \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{m}{1\ \mathrm{g}}\right).$$

The gravity wall has the form $m=(c^2/2G)r$. Taking the logarithm turns
multiplication into addition. Using the numerical values of the constants in
grams and centimetres:

$$y = x + \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{c^2}{2G}\right)
   = x + 27.83.$$

The coefficient of $x$ is **+1**, so increasing radius by one order of
magnitude increases the limiting mass by one order of magnitude. The
intercept is **27.83**: when $r=1$ cm and therefore $x=0$, the line gives
$m=6.73\times10^{27}$ g.

The quantum wall has the form $m=(\hbar/c)r^{-1}$. Taking the logarithm gives

$$y = -x + \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\hbar}{c}\right)
   = -x - 37.45.$$

The coefficient of $x$ is **−1**, so increasing radius by one order of
magnitude decreases the limiting mass by one order of magnitude. Its
intercept is **−37.45**: at $r=1$ cm, the line gives
$m=3.52\times10^{-38}$ g.

The slopes express the exponents of $r$ and do not depend on the chosen units.
The intercepts come from $G$, $c$ and $\hbar$ and **do** shift if the axes use
different units.
:::

```{pyodide}
def schwarzschild_mass(r):   # heaviest object of radius r (it's a black hole)
    return r * c**2 / (2 * G)

def compton_mass(r):         # lightest object of radius r (quantum limit)
    return hbar / (r * c)

wall_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": r_line,
    "gravity_mass_g": schwarzschild_mass(r_line),
    "compton_mass_g": compton_mass(r_line),
    "upper_mass_g": 1e60,
    "lower_mass_g": 1e-40,
})

gravity_region = alt.Chart(wall_data).mark_area(
    color="#e66852", opacity=0.15, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(),
    y=cosmos_y("gravity_mass_g"),
    y2=alt.Y2("upper_mass_g:Q"),
)

quantum_region = alt.Chart(wall_data).mark_area(
    color="#4269d0", opacity=0.15, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(),
    y=cosmos_y("lower_mass_g"),
    y2=alt.Y2("compton_mass_g:Q"),
)

wall_lines = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({"radius_cm": r_line,
                  "mass_g": schwarzschild_mass(r_line),
                  "wall": "black-hole limit"}),
    pd.DataFrame({"radius_cm": r_line,
                  "mass_g": compton_mass(r_line),
                  "wall": "Compton limit"}),
], ignore_index=True)

wall_line_chart = alt.Chart(wall_lines).mark_line(
    color="#171717", strokeWidth=1.5, clip=True
).encode(
    x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), detail="wall:N"
)

gravity_label = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": [3e-14], "mass_g": [1e45],
    "label": ["forbidden by gravity"],
})).mark_text(
    angle=322, color="#8a3324", fontSize=14
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

quantum_label = alt.Chart(pd.DataFrame({
    "radius_cm": [3e-5], "mass_g": [1e-36],
    "label": ["quantum uncertainty"],
})).mark_text(
    angle=38, color="#1d3f8f", fontSize=14
).encode(x=cosmos_x(), y=cosmos_y(), text="label:N")

(
    gravity_region
    + quantum_region
    + wall_line_chart
    + object_layers(point_size=75)
    + gravity_label
    + quantum_label
).properties(
    width="container",
    height=700,
    title="29 objects",
).configure_axis(
    gridColor="#dddddd",
    gridOpacity=0.7,
    labelFontSize=13,
    labelPadding=6,
    titleFontSize=16,
    titlePadding=14,
).configure_title(
    fontSize=20,
    anchor="middle",
    offset=16,
)
```

The empty corners of Step 2 are now explained and shaded.
They are empty because they are **impossible**.

The *absence* of data carries a claim from physics. The claim is encoded by the shading.

Note the object in the top-right corner:

```{pyodide}
iU = names.index("observable Universe")
ratio = 2 * G * mass[iU] / c**2 / radius[iU]
print(f"Universe: Schwarzschild radius / actual radius = {ratio:.2f}")
```

```{pyodide}
assert 0.8 < ratio < 1.2
print("✓ the observable Universe sits ON the black-hole line")
```

The Universe's mass and radius satisfy the black-hole relation almost
exactly.

Does that mean we live inside a black hole? Read what the paper has to say about this!

## 5 · The Planck scale

The walls of slope +1 and −1 meet at a crossing point:

$$\frac{rc^2}{2G} = \frac{\hbar}{rc}
\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;
r = \sqrt{\frac{2G\hbar}{c^3}},\qquad
m = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar c}{2G}}.$$

```{pyodide}
r_x = np.sqrt(2 * G * hbar / c**3)
m_x = np.sqrt(hbar * c / (2 * G))
l_p = np.sqrt(hbar * G / c**3)    # Planck length
m_p = np.sqrt(hbar * c / G)       # Planck mass

print(f"walls cross at    r = {r_x:.2e} cm,  m = {m_x:.2e} g")
print(f"Planck scale:   l_p = {l_p:.2e} cm, m_p = {m_p:.2e} g")
```

```{pyodide}
assert abs(r_x / (np.sqrt(2) * l_p) - 1) < 1e-6
assert abs(m_x / (m_p / np.sqrt(2)) - 1) < 1e-6
print("✓ the walls cross at the Planck scale (times a factor of √2)")
```

The crossing point is the **Planck scale**: about $10^{-33}$ cm and
$2\times10^{-5}$ g. The smallest possible object is a
Planck-mass black hole, which the paper calls an **instanton**: the only
thing that is simultaneously as small as gravity allows and as small as
quantum mechanics allows.

Left of the Planck length, physics has no
tested theory at all (the paper shades it "sub-Planckian unknown").

#### Place the Universe

Derive the Universe's point (given to you in the table).

The radius of the observable Universe is the
Hubble radius $r_H = c/H_0$. Its average density is the critical density
$\rho_c = 3H_0^2 / 8\pi G$. Its mass is that density times the volume
of the Hubble sphere. Does your derived Universe lands on
the black-hole line?

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_hubble
import numpy as np
G    = 6.674e-8       # [cm^3 g^-1 s^-2]
c    = 2.998e10       # [cm/s]
H0   = 70 / 3.086e19  # [1/s]
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_hubble
# Constants G, c and H0 are loaded (cgs units).
# 1. Hubble radius, critical density, and the mass of the Hubble sphere.
# 2. Schwarzschild radius of that mass: how does it compare to r_H?

r_H   = ______
rho_c = ______
m_U   = ______

r_s = 2 * G * m_U / c**2
print(f"r_H = {r_H:.2e} cm   m_U = {m_U:.2e} g")
print(f"Schwarzschild radius of the Universe's mass: {r_s:.2e} cm")
print(f"ratio r_s / r_H = {r_s / r_H:.3f}")
```

:::

Before drawing your chart, open Lineweaver and Patel's
[*All objects and some questions*](https://doi.org/10.1119/5.0150209) and
study Figure 2. Look at how the authors use points, direct labels, boundary
lines, shaded regions and annotation to explain the mass–radius space. Decide
which of those choices help the claims you want your version to support.
:::

Build your own **Triangle of Everything** using Altair (or another library of your choice).
Your final chart should
include:

- logarithmic mass and radius axes with readable titles and tick labels;
- all 29 objects, labelled and coloured by group;
- the atomic-density and nuclear-density reference lines;
- the gravity and quantum walls, with the impossible regions shaded;
- the sub-Planckian region and the Planck-scale instanton; and
- a clear title, legend and annotations that make the chart interpretable
  without referring back to the code.

## Sources

- Lineweaver, C. H. & Patel, V. M. (2023) *All objects and some
  questions*, American Journal of Physics 91:819–825
  ([doi:10.1119/5.0150209](https://doi.org/10.1119/5.0150209)), the
  original Figure 2, which this page rebuilds in simplified form (we omit
  the cosmological-epoch background shading and plot a smaller object
  sample).
- `objects_universe.csv` is curated for this course: masses and radii are
  order-of-magnitude values assembled from standard references; the
  human and whale entries deliberately reproduce the paper's values,
  sphericity and all. Fundamental particles are plotted at their Compton
  wavelengths (the proton at its measured charge radius); black holes at
  their Schwarzschild radii.
- Constants: CODATA values rounded to 4 significant figures;
  $H_0 = 70$ km/s/Mpc.
